analysis.one_liner: Bars hospitals and doctors from surprise-billing patients for emergency and in-network care.
analysis.headline: The bill won no Republican support and never left a House subcommittee, dying when the 115th Congress ended with hospitals still free to send surprise bills.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Billing Act of 2017 would stop hospitals that are in an insurer's network — and the doctors practicing inside them — from billing a patient more than the normal in-network copay, and would apply the same rule to emergency care no matter where it happens. It would set up an independent review process to settle payment disputes between insurers and providers, and authorize $4 billion in grants to help states run those reviews. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with health coverage gain the most: someone treated at an in-network hospital could no longer be handed an extra bill from an out-of-network doctor working there, and someone in an emergency room could not be charged out-of-network rates at all, except when they got advance written notice and consented. Insurers also gain a cap on their exposure to disputed out-of-network charges, since an independent expert would set what they must pay. States gain access to $4 billion in federal grants to run the review process [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing surprise hospital bills

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals in a patient's insurance network — and every provider practicing inside them — could no longer bill the patient more than the normal in-network cost sharing
For emergency care, the hospital and any doctors involved could not charge more than in-network cost sharing, regardless of network status
An independent health care expert would settle payment disputes between insurers and providers, notify the patient within 30 days, and count any patient cost sharing toward the annual deductible
States electing to run the review process would get a share of $4 billion in federal grant money, with the federal government stepping in for states that opt out

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and out-of-network physicians lose the ability to balance-bill patients for care at in-network facilities and for emergencies; insurers would owe payment on those cases as set by the review process; and taxpayers would fund up to $4 billion in state grants (the bill authorizes but does not directly appropriate the money) [S3].

drawbacks.text: The protection is not absolute: a provider could still charge out-of-network rates if it gave the patient a cost estimate and obtained written consent 72 hours ahead of scheduled care (24 hours on short notice), meaning the surprise-billing ban has a built-in opt-out

The payment methodology tilts toward providers: the reviewer would generally pay the lower of the provider's proposed charge or the 80th percentile of what all payers report paying — a high benchmark — and could never pay less than 1.25 times the Medicare rate
The bill authorizes $4 billion in federal grants to states, a real taxpayer cost to administer a dispute process, on top of shifting payment for out-of-network care from patients to insurers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core consumer protections were real and aimed at one of the most resented billing practices in American health care, and the $4 billion grant program was modest relative to the scale of surprise billing. The honest objections are the written-consent loophole, which preserves a path for providers to surprise-bill people who sign forms they may not fully understand, and an arbitration formula keyed to the 80th percentile of all-payer charges that would likely push payment rates up rather than down. On balance the bill helped patients more than it cost anyone else, which makes its quiet death in subcommittee more consequential.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, passed down to a health subcommittee, and stayed there until the 115th Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Michelle Lujan Grisham introduced the Fair Billing Act of 2017 on September 28, 2017, with 5 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and a day later it went to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and out-of-network physicians came out ahead: without this law they kept the ability to send patients surprise bills for care at in-network facilities and emergencies, and insurers never took on the new payment obligations the review process would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and out-of-network physicians who balance-bill

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote its surprise-billing protections, review process, and state grant program

for.name: 5 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only supporters were 6 House Democrats — the sponsor and 5 cosponsors, with no Republican cosponsor — but it never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill takes away the practice of balance-billing patients for out-of-network care delivered at in-network hospitals and in emergencies — a practice whose entire value to these providers comes from charging patients more than their insurance expects. The review process cushions the loss with a payment floor of 1.25 times Medicare rates and an 80th-percentile benchmark that is generous by later standards.

Insurers would have to participate in the review process and pay whatever the independent expert sets for disputed out-of-network care, but in exchange the amounts are capped and their members are shielded from balance bills that often create disputes between plans and providers.
States electing to run the review process would get federal grants from a $4 billion authorization, with HHS running the process in states that decline.
